sentences.text: Platypterygius is a genus of Cretaceous ichthyosaurs, a group of marine reptiles, with a name meaning "flat fin".
Species assigned to this genus were generally large-bodied macropredators that reached a length of approximately 7 meters, possessing a long snout and a powerful tail equipped with fins.
Unlike most ichthyosaurs, Platypterygius had more digits in its forefins than is usual for the group.
Several species of Platypterygius include described specimens of juveniles, newborns, and pregnant females.
In 2010, Zammit and colleagues estimated that P. australis was about 7 meters long.
While fossils of Platypterygius have been found on different continents, the holotype specimen — the specimen the species is based on — was discovered in Germany.
The type species was described in 1922 based on remains from Germany that had previously been described as Ichthyosaurus platydactylus in 1907 by Ferdinand Broili.
Unfortunately, the original remains used to describe the type species were not adequately described and were destroyed during World War 2.
Like other ichthyosaurs, Platypterygius was viviparous, meaning it gave birth to live young rather than laying eggs.
Fossil evidence from P. australis includes hatchling protostegid sea turtles and enantiornithine birds found alongside fish in its gut contents.
A specimen of P. australis from Australia preserved gut contents of cephalopods, fish, and pterosaurs, as well as bite marks likely made by Kronosaurus queenslandicus.
Platypterygius was historically used as a wastebasket taxon, with many species likely being undiagnostic or representing distinct genera.
Research in the 2000s and 2010s showed that the defining features of Platypterygius were either not present in all assigned species or were also found in other ophthalmosaurids.
An analysis by Zverkov and Jacobs (2020) showed that P. americanus is too distantly related to other species within the genus.
Platypterygius is the genus most closely related to Caypullisaurus and Brachypterygius.
Platypterygius lived during the Late Aptian to Late Cenomanian stages in the Early Cretaceous in what is now Australia, Russia, the United States, Germany, and possibly New Zealand.
The time range for Platypterygius is estimated from 161.5 to 93.9 million years ago.
The interpretation that a specific P. australis specimen preserved gut contents is contested by some researchers.
